opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it came down to what felt meaningful to me. Drilling problems has diminishing returns. Once you understand a type of question, doing the hundredth variation mostly trains speed and stamina. That matters for the exam, but it didn't feel like I was growing. Learning something new, whether a branch of math or some programming, gave me that feeling of a door opening. I could feel my understanding of the world expanding, and that was far more motivating than shaving a few seconds off a familiar problem.

There was also a practical side. I noticed that when I truly understood the underlying concepts, a lot of exam problems became easier anyway. Going a bit deeper or broader gave me a higher vantage point, so I didn't need as much repetition. Of course you still need some practice to stay sharp, and I'm not saying drilling is useless. But I tried to do just enough to stay reliable and spend the rest of my energy on learning.

Looking back, I think that habit shaped how I approach research too. In fields like AI systems, things change so fast that the skill that matters most is picking up new areas quickly, not perfecting one fixed routine. So in a way, preferring to learn new things wasn't only about exams. It was the beginning of how I like to work.

r001.rationale: The response says that learning more deeply or broadly built conceptual understanding and a higher vantage point, making exam problems easier without relying on repetitive drilling.

r002.rationale: It does not say Kaichao You’s entrance exam was relatively easy or that this kept his ability to solve difficult problems from showing in his score.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it came down to what felt rewarding at the time. When you drill problems for the gaokao, you're mostly repeating the same patterns over and over, and after a certain point the marginal gain is tiny. You might go from 95 percent to 97 percent, but you spend enormous effort for that. For me, that felt like a bad trade.

Learning something new, on the other hand, gave me a much stronger sense of progress. I remember picking up things that weren't on the syllabus at all, just because I was curious. Every day you learn something new, you feel like you actually grew. With drilling, you don't feel that. You just feel tired.

There was also a bit of a strategic thought behind it, even though I probably couldn't have articulated it clearly back then. I believed that if I really understood the underlying ideas, the problems would take care of themselves. If you know why something works, you can handle a question even if it's phrased in a way you haven't seen before. If you've only memorized the pattern, a small twist can throw you off. So in my mind, understanding was the more robust strategy, not just the more enjoyable one.

Of course, there's a risk. Teachers and parents will tell you that this is not how you maximize your score, and they're partly right. Some of my classmates who drilled very hard did score higher than me on certain tests. But I never regretted it, because the habit of chasing new knowledge instead of chasing points is what stayed with me afterward. In university and later in research, nobody gives you a problem set with a known answer. The only thing that carries over is your curiosity and your ability to learn things on your own. So in hindsight, I think I was training the right muscle, even if it wasn't the most efficient one for the exam itself.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts repetitive drilling with learning underlying ideas, saying deeper understanding helps handle unfamiliar twists that memorized patterns cannot.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not say the entrance exam was relatively easy or that its ease kept Kaichao’s ability to solve difficult problems from showing in his score.
